text.en: One day Raman and Sheela wrote how they spent their day. Raman used circles, one for each hour. Sheela drew tall bars. Both show the same kind of facts, but Sheela's way is called a bar graph.

Raman recorded his routine in a table with one circle for each hour: sleeping, school, studying, eating and playing and other activities.
Sheela drew vertical bars. The vertical line shows the number of hours and the horizontal base shows the different activities.
The taller the bar, the more hours were spent on that activity.
To read a bar graph, find the top of a bar and look across to the number on the vertical line.
Compare bars to answer questions: who sleeps more, who spends more hours in school and how many more hours Sheela studies than Raman.
To make your own bar graph: write the activities on the base, mark the hours on the vertical line, and draw a bar of equal width up to the right height for each activity. You can use paper strips pasted along the base to compare finger lengths.
A pictograph shows data with icons; a bar graph shows data with bars. Both help us see and compare quickly.

problem.en: A bar for studying reaches 4 and a bar for eating and playing reaches 3. Which is more and by how much?

text.en: Read the top of each bar on the vertical line: 4 and 3.

why.en: Look across from the top of the bar.

prompt.en: How do you read the height of a bar in a bar graph?

requiredIdeas.en: Look at the top of the bar
Read across to the vertical line

commonMisconceptions.en: Reading the base instead of the vertical line

points.en: A bar graph uses bars of equal width; taller bars mean more.
The vertical line shows the number and the base shows the groups.
Compare bars by subtracting their heights.
We can make a bar graph of our own day.
